summary: Defines an XML format for a permission document used to request consent. A relay uses a document in this format to ask a specific recipient for permission to perform a particular routing translation. It is a standards-track document that supports the SIP consent framework.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the standard form a messenger fills out to ask someone, may I pass messages to you on behalf of others? The person can then answer yes or no.

questions: what is a sip permission document
what is trans-handling in sip consent
subtitle: An XML format a SIP relay uses to ask a recipient whether it may forward requests to them.

tldr.problem: A SIP relay that translates one address into others needs a standard way to ask a recipient for permission before it sends them requests.
tldr.mechanism: The permission document is an XML document built on Common Policy. It adds recipient and target conditions and a trans-handling action that carries URIs for granting or denying the translation.
tldr.outcome: It supplies the document format for the SIP consent framework of RFC 5360. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5361 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the document format for the consent framework of RFC 5360.

sections.title: The Permission Document
sections.content:
The SIP consent framework in RFC 5360 needs a format for permission documents. A SIP relay, meaning any SIP server (proxy, B2BUA or a hybrid) that receives a request and translates its Request-URI into one or more next-hop URIs, uses such a document to ask for permission to perform a translation.

RFC 5361 defines that format. It is based on Common Policy (RFC 4745), an XML format for privacy preferences. The terms target URI (the Request-URI of the incoming request) and recipient URI (the Request-URI of the outgoing request) come from RFC 5360.
sections.plainLanguage: A messenger who passes notes on behalf of others must first ask each person for permission. This is the form for asking.

sections.title: Structure of the Document
sections.content:
A permission document is an XML document that follows the Common Policy schema and has the MIME type application/auth-policy+xml. Like any Common Policy document it has conditions, actions and transformations. This RFC defines new conditions and actions but no new transformation.

A document applies to a translation only if all expressions in its conditions evaluate to TRUE. The new elements live in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:consent-rules namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: The slip has three boxes: who it is about, what you are allowed to do, and extra changes. This slip leaves the third box empty.

sections.title: Conditions
sections.content:
The recipient condition is matched against the recipient URI. When a grant or deny arrives, for example in a SIP PUBLISH request, the relay matches it against the identity of whoever sent that answer. The target condition is matched against the target URI, normally the Request-URI of the incoming request. The identity condition, from Common Policy, is matched against the sender of the request being translated. Recipient and target conditions accept the same elements and attributes as identity conditions, and the id attribute of one and except in a permission document MUST contain a scheme.

Only authenticated identities can match. The accepted means are SIP Identity, P-Asserted-Identity (closed networks only), SIP digest and, for answers, a return routability test, which has no identity matching. A digest request with an anonymous username is unauthenticated, but a validated Identity header on a From of the form sip:anonymous@example.com counts as authenticated.

The validity and sphere elements are not applicable and MUST be ignored if present. Permissions have an infinite lifetime and are revoked by an independent mechanism described in RFC 5360.
sections.plainLanguage: The slip says who the messenger is passing notes to, which address the notes are sent to, and optionally who is allowed to send them. Only people who can prove who they are count.

sections.title: Actions: Granting and Denying
sections.content:
The trans-handling element is informational rather than a Common Policy action, so conflict resolution does not apply to it. Each rule contains at least two such elements, one with a URI to grant and one with a URI to deny. Its value is either grant, telling the relay to perform the translation, or deny, telling it not to. The required perm-uri attribute holds the URI the recipient uses to give that answer.

In the RFC's example, a client adds sip:bob@example.org to the translation whose target is sip:alices-friends@example.com. The relay builds a document with the recipient and target conditions, two grant URIs and two deny URIs (a sips: and an https: form of each), and sends it to Bob.
sections.plainLanguage: The slip contains one link for "yes" and one for "no". Bob picks one, and the messenger knows what to do.

sections.title: Extensibility, IANA and Security
sections.content:
The defined elements have no extension points. Instances SHOULD be schema valid, and applications MUST ignore content they do not understand. Later IETF documents MAY reuse the consent-rules namespace to add elements.

IANA registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:consent-rules and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:consent-rules. The security section only points to RFC 5360, which covers how to authenticate SIP and HTTP requests that grant permissions and how to transport permission documents between relays and recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: If the form has extra writing the reader does not understand, they just skip it. The rules about keeping the form safe are in a different document.
